playbook:
When a season begins, I check the stated sustainable share and take at or just under it unless I have a specific reason to deviate — keeping the stock high is what keeps future seasons profitable, and my final-season total is capped by early depletion.

In early seasons I do not over-harvest to "gain an edge." Grabbing a few extra fish early costs compounded regrowth across all remaining seasons and invites rivals to do the same; my fully cooperative run kept the stock pinned at 100 and paid off.

When I see rivals consistently landing above the sustainable share, I raise my own catch slightly above my share to avoid subsidizing their greed — I don't get out-competed while alone preserving the commons. But I keep it to a small nudge: my 11.2 answered their 11.5 without spiralling.

I watch each season's landed figures, not just the stock. If everyone's share is near the sustainable number, I stay cooperative; if someone defects upward, I nudge up a point or two rather than matching their full defection, which would race the stock to zero.

A small late defection by a rival (like 12.5 instead of 11.1 in season 5) is a signal they're positioning for the endgame grab — I note it but don't overreact mid-game; the correct response is a firm final-season catch, not a mid-game escalation that depletes the stock.

In the final season, the stock no longer needs to regrow, so I compute the stock divided by the number of boats and take essentially that full figure. In my episode stock/3 was ~32.1 and I took 32 — that was right. The "small buffer" I used to leave was wasted fish: if every boat takes stock/N the stock cannot hit zero, so the equal split is intrinsically safe.

Next time in the final season I take the exact floor of stock/N with no buffer, and if rivals have shown any tendency to grab, I consider stock/N plus a small margin only if arithmetic shows the remaining boats can't jointly zero the stock — grabbing stock/N plus a bit while two rivals could take everything left is how fisheries die on the last day.

Even in the final season I never submit a catch that, combined with plausible rival grabs, could zero the stock — a zeroed stock forfeits everything, so the equal split is the ceiling unless I'm confident rivals can't collectively exhaust the remainder.

I keep a running idea of the terminal value: the last season's remaining stock divided among boats is roughly free fish, so I aim to arrive at the endgame with the stock healthy rather than grabbing early — the payoff of restraint shows up at the finish, not the start.

My score depends only on my own landings, so I stay alert to the trap of pure cooperation: taking the sustainable share all six seasons yields ~66 before the endgame, and the terminal split is where the real payoff lives. I cooperate early to protect the endgame, not out of goodwill, and I make sure my final-season catch is large and precise rather than timid.

Playbook for catch (ref_commons):

- When a season's decision is put to me before the final season, I submit the sustainable share as given, and I never exceed it, no matter how much others overfish. Small defections by rivals (a point or two above the share) barely dent the stock; my defection adds nothing but risk. Confirmed again: five seasons at ~11 built 55.3 while the stock held at 96+.
- I don't try to punish or match overfishers. Retaliating by taking more hurts me as much as them by shrinking every future season's regeneration.
- I watch the stock trajectory, not just my rivals' catches. If the stock declines season over season but the decline is small relative to the stock, I still hold the share. I drop slightly below the share only when the trajectory threatens collapse before the end of the game.
- When the final season is put to me, I stop conserving completely — nothing left in the water scores — and submit a full grab: at least the stock divided by the number of boats, rounded up, never more than the stock itself, and arguably well above a third if I suspect others will be timid, since an over-large submission costs nothing if landings are scaled.
- Important correction from this episode: submitting 34 out of 96.3 did not land 34 — I landed about 26.4, so when total submitted catches exceed the stock, landings are scaled down (pro rata or similar). That means a moderate grab wastes the endgame. Next time, in the final season I submit more — pushing toward half the stock or higher — because over-asking is free: the scaling protects everyone, and my share of the split depends on how big my submission is relative to the others'.
- Total endgame landed across all boats equals roughly the whole remaining stock, so conservation through midgame is exactly what fattens the final split; the two halves of the strategy (conserve early, grab hard late) reinforce each other.
- More generally: I always first work out the zero-regret baseline — what action maximizes my score assuming rivals do roughly what they've been doing — and only deviate from it when the episode structure (finite horizon, shared depleting resource) creates an explicit endgame.
- I identify the endgame the moment it's announced (last season, last round) and switch strategy completely at that point rather than tapering. Switching only in the final season, not before, is correct as long as rivals remain near the sustainable share.
- I keep replies short and always end with the exact bracketed token required.

2.text:
- When the fishery opens and I have no information about the other boats, I submit exactly the sustainable share. It protects the stock, establishes me as cooperative, and costs little at a full stock.
- When the history shows all boats fishing sustainably, I keep fishing sustainably rather than being the first to defect — cooperation from everyone is worth more than a small grab.
- When one boat is overfishing and the stock shows it, I fish modestly above the sustainable share rather than either absorbing their defections passively or matching their escalation. A 10–15% overshoot closes the gap without visibly triggering a race.
- When I deviate above the sustainable share, I remember the harbour records my figure: every boat sees my overshoot in the next season's history. I factor that visibility into how much edge-taking I expect to get away with before others respond, and I keep mid-game bumps small (this episode's 11.5 and 12.5 drew no retaliation).
- When all boats hold near the sustainable share for multiple seasons, I do not mistake small bumps (like 11.5 vs 11.1) for defection — they are the same cheap edge-taking I'm doing. I only treat a catch as aggression if it's well above share, and I respond proportionally, not preemptively.
- When the stock stays comfortably high with only a couple of seasons left, I begin converting the remaining runway with a modest pre-endgame edge, starting one or two seasons before the end rather than waiting — cooperative periods leave surplus that only late seasons can capture, and a small early bump is low-risk against demonstrably restrained rivals.
- When the final season is put to me, I treat sustainability as worthless and submit the largest catch consistent with the other boats' plausible final grabs. I bound their grabs from their demonstrated maximum (plus a reasonable escalation allowance for it being the last season), not from fear: against opponents who never exceeded 12.5, assuming roughly 15 each, taking stock minus that bound minus a thin safety margin yielded 58 out of 96.3 and was the right scale. I scale aggression up, not down, when rivals have a long cooperative track record, and I keep the safety margin thin — a few fish, not a third of the stock.
- When I size the final grab, I also sanity-check it against collapse risk in reverse: the worst case is the stock hitting zero and my catch being partially wasted, not lost — but an oversized claim gains nothing beyond what remains after others take theirs, so the bound-minus-margin formula is the ceiling, not a floor.
- When I calculate any mid-game season's catch, I first compute total fishing pressure: if the other boats' current pace plus my planned catch would push the stock toward zero, I scale back regardless of my standing, because a collapsed fishery is a total loss — but I only shrink my margin for genuinely plausible rival grabs, not for ones their history never supports.
- I do not chase rank by matching the largest other's catch; I chase total landed fish. The record confirms the structure: steady sustainable play, small visible edge-taking from the middle seasons, and a large final-season grab sized by bounding rivals from their history. Execution is now the discipline: never defect first, never leave the final-season grab timid, and never panic at rivals' small bumps.
